Indirect Effects in a lavaan Model with ci()

Source: vignettes/articles/indirect-effects-lavaan.Rmd
indirect-effects-lavaan.Rmd

ci(fit) on a lavaan fit gives an interval for every defined parameter (:=) in one call. This page walks through a model with several mediators, shows which method each indirect effect gets, and ends with a small helper that puts every result in one table. The rules behind the choices are in Technical Notes, section 7, and the one-page version is in the Quick Reference.

1. A model with two mediators

The data have x -> m1 -> m2 -> y, a direct x -> m2 path, and direct paths from both mediators to y. Four indirect effects are of interest: through m1 alone, through m2 alone, the serial path through both, and their sum.

set.seed(11)
n <- 500
d <- data.frame(x = rnorm(n))
d$m1 <- 0.5 * d$x + rnorm(n)
d$m2 <- 0.3 * d$x + 0.4 * d$m1 + rnorm(n)
d$y <- 0.3 * d$m1 + 0.4 * d$m2 + 0.1 * d$x + rnorm(n)

model <- "
  m1 ~ a1*x
  m2 ~ a2*x + d*m1
  y  ~ b1*m1 + b2*m2 + cp*x
  via_m1 := a1*b1
  via_m2 := a2*b2
  serial := a1*d*b2
  total  := a1*b1 + a2*b2 + a1*d*b2
"
fit <- lavaan::sem(model, d)

2. One call, four intervals 

set.seed(1)
res <- ci(fit, n.mc = 20000)
names(res)
#> [1] "via_m1" "via_m2" "serial" "total"

Each definition gets the method that fits its form:

Definition Form Method
via_m1 := a1*b1, via_m2 := a2*b2 two coefficients distribution of the product, or the type you ask for
serial := a1*d*b2 three different coefficients the exact three-factor interval, whatever type is
total := a1*b1 + a2*b2 + a1*d*b2 a sum, not a product Monte Carlo on the formula

A product of four or more different coefficients also gets Monte Carlo. Because the methods differ, the entries do not have the same shape:

vapply(res, function(z) paste(names(z), collapse = ", "), character(1))
#>                       via_m1                       via_m2 
#>           "CI, Estimate, SE"           "CI, Estimate, SE" 
#>                       serial                        total 
#>               "lower, upper" ", Estimate, SE, MCError, p"

The exact interval is a bare named vector, lower and upper; the others are lists with an interval first.

3. One table for all of them

This helper reads the interval from either shape, takes each estimate from lavaan itself, and labels the route:

tidy_ci <- function(res, fit) {
  est <- lavaan::parameterEstimates(fit)
  est <- est[est$op == ":=", c("lhs", "est")]
  rows <- lapply(names(res), function(lab) {
    r <- res[[lab]]
    exact <- !is.list(r)
    bounds <- if (exact) as.numeric(r[c("lower", "upper")]) else as.numeric(r[[1]])
    route <- if (exact) {
      "exact, three factors"
    } else if ("MC.Error" %in% names(r)) {
      "Monte Carlo, product"
    } else if ("MCError" %in% names(r)) {
      "Monte Carlo, formula"
    } else {
      "distribution of the product"
    }
    data.frame(
      parameter = lab, estimate = est$est[est$lhs == lab],
      lower = bounds[1], upper = bounds[2], route = route
    )
  })
  do.call(rbind, rows)
}

out <- tidy_ci(res, fit)
out[2:4] <- round(out[2:4], 4)
out
#>   parameter estimate  lower  upper                       route
#> 1    via_m1   0.1500 0.0978 0.2072 distribution of the product
#> 2    via_m2   0.1109 0.0661 0.1610 distribution of the product
#> 3    serial   0.0870 0.0594 0.1195        exact, three factors
#> 4     total   0.3479 0.2771 0.4245        Monte Carlo, formula

4. Check the exact interval against Monte Carlo

The exact interval for serial and a large Monte Carlo run on the same estimates should agree to within simulation error:

set.seed(2)
mc <- ci(fit, type = "MC", n.mc = 2e5)
round(rbind(exact = res$serial[c("lower", "upper")], monte_carlo = mc$serial[[1]]), 4)
#>              lower  upper
#> exact       0.0594 0.1195
#> monte_carlo 0.0594 0.1196

type = "MC" is used as asked for every definition, so mc$serial is a Monte Carlo interval here.

5. What the warnings mean

You get a warning only when you set type yourself and RMediation uses a different method for a definition. With the default type, nothing is said.

tryCatch(
  ci(fit, type = "dop", n.mc = 2000),
  warning = function(w) conditionMessage(w)
)
#> [1] "Defined parameter 'total' is not a product of estimated coefficients; using a Monte Carlo interval instead of type = \"dop\"."

The same applies to a three-coefficient product when you ask for "asymp", "prodclin" or "all" (the exact interval does not depend on type), and to a product of four or more coefficients.

6. Cases to know

  • A sum, a constant or a sign (a*b + c, 2*a*b, -a*b, a*b/2) is not a plain product of coefficients, so it takes the Monte Carlo route on the formula.
  • A repeated coefficient inside a product of three or more (a*b*a) cannot use the exact interval, because the factors are perfectly correlated. Releases up to 1.10.0 stop on it for every type except "MC"; 1.11.0 uses Monte Carlo and warns when you chose another type. A repeated coefficient in a product of two (a*a) is fine.
  • The p in a formula-route result. A Monte Carlo interval on a formula carries a p element: twice the smaller share of simulated values above or below 0. It shows where the sampling distribution of the estimate sits relative to 0, it is exactly 0 for any clearly nonzero effect, and it is not a test against a null distribution; do not report it as one (use mbco() for that). The exact three-factor interval has no p.
  • A definition that cannot be resolved (a cycle, or text that does not parse) gets a warning and a NULL entry under its label, and every other interval is still returned.
  • Seeds. Monte Carlo results change from run to run. Call set.seed() before ci() and report it; see Reporting RMediation in a Paper.
